parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a lakeside holiday park to book a cabin for a week in June.
script: Good morning, Lakeview Holiday Park, Hannah speaking.
Oh, good morning. I'd like to book a cabin for a week in June, please, if you've got anything left.
Of course. Let me just bring up the booking screen. We're quite busy that month, but I'm sure we can find you something. Could I take your name first?
Sorry, could you spell the surname for me?
Pettifer. Thank you, Mr Pettifer. And a contact number?
My mobile's the best one. It's 07741 380 296.
07741 380 296. Lovely. Now, when were you thinking of arriving?
I was hoping for a Thursday, if that's possible, because the roads are quieter in the middle of the week.
Ah, I'm afraid I can't do Thursday. All our cabins change over on Fridays. You can arrive from 3 o'clock in the afternoon, and everybody has to be out by 10 on the day they leave.
I see. Well, in that case Friday's fine. We're not in any hurry.
And how many nights would you like? A full week?
Well, we'd said 7, but my wife's just reminded me that she's got a hospital appointment the Friday after that, so we'd better make it 6 nights.
6 nights, so you'd be leaving on a Thursday. That's no problem at all.
Now, our cabins are all named after birds. The Kingfisher is the one people ask for most, because it's right beside the water.
I'm afraid it's already taken for those dates, though. I can offer you the Heron, which is next door and has exactly the same view of the lake.
Then the Heron, please. That'll be fine.
Is there anyone in your party with any special requirements?
Yes, there'll be 5 of us, including my mother. She's 84 and she finds stairs very difficult, so we'd need a bedroom on the ground floor.
That's no trouble. The Heron has a double bedroom downstairs with its own shower room. I'll make a note of it.
Wonderful. Oh, and we'd like to hire something to use on the lake. What do you have?
Kayaks are 20 pounds for the day, and bicycles are 12 pounds. We also have rowing boats, which are 15 pounds.
The grandchildren would love the kayaks, but I don't think my knees would cope. Let's go for a rowing boat, then. We can all fit in one. Could you reserve it for the Saturday?
Of course. I've put that on the booking.
Now, what's the price of the cabin, please?
The Heron is 95 pounds a night in June. It goes up to 130 pounds in July and August, so you're just in time before the summer rates start.
We ask for a deposit of 20 percent to confirm the booking, and the balance is due 4 weeks before you arrive.
Right. Can I pay the deposit by card now?
Yes, if you like. Or I can email you a link and you can do it this evening, whichever you prefer.
I'll do it now, if that's all right. Here's my card.

Thank you. That's gone through. Now, just one last thing. Bed linen is included and the beds will be made up when you arrive, so you don't need to bring sheets. You do need to bring your own towels, though. We only provide tea towels.
Towels. Right, I'll tell my wife, she's the one who does the packing.
And do you have a dog with you? Dogs are welcome, but they must be kept on a lead.
Lovely. Is there anything else I can help you with?
Is there a shop on the site? I'd rather not stop on the way.
There is, next to reception. It sells milk, bread and newspapers from 8 every morning, so you don't need to bring much food with you on the first day.
That's very helpful. Thank you very much, Hannah.
You're welcome, Mr Pettifer. I'll send the confirmation to your email address, and we look forward to seeing you in June.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A volunteer coordinator welcomes new volunteers to a community garden.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome. Do grab a cup of tea if you haven't already, there's plenty in the pot. My name's Dan Kowalski, and I'm the volunteer coordinator here at Fernbank Community Garden. It's great to see so many new faces.

Let me start with a little history, because it helps to explain why we do things the way we do. Fifteen years ago, this whole site was a rubbish-strewn patch of ground behind the old bus depot. A lot of people assume the council set up the garden, because it owned the land, but in fact it had no plans for it at all. It was a group of residents from the flats opposite who got together, borrowed a few spades and cleared it themselves. The primary school over the road joined in a few years later, which is why you'll see the children's beds near the gate, but it's still the residents who run things today.

Now, money. We did receive a government grant to build the greenhouse, but that was a one-off, and it finished two years ago. Local businesses are very generous with donations of compost and tools, but that doesn't pay the water bill. What really keeps us going is the stall at the front gate. We sell vegetables, herbs and young plants every Saturday, and that brings in most of what we need each year.

Before you pick up a fork or a trowel, there's one thing everybody has to do, and that's come along to a short safety talk. It takes about 40 minutes, and I run it on Monday evenings at 6.30. We talk about tools and lifting. You don't need a health check.  And you don't have to buy gloves either, because we keep a whole box of them in the shed.

Another thing. If you can't make one of your sessions, please don't ring me. I'm usually up to my elbows in compost and I never hear the phone, and email just gets lost in my inbox. The best thing by far is to post a message in the volunteers' group chat. Somebody will always be able to cover for you, and I'll see it too. I'll give you the link at the end.

Now, one of the perks. When the stall closes on a Saturday, any vegetables that haven't sold are bagged up, and volunteers can take a bag home. You can't just help yourself to whatever's growing, I'm afraid, because that would cause chaos, and the seeds are sold rather than given away. But we do hold a free seed swap in March, so do come along to that.

Right, let me tell you about the weekly timetable, because each session has a different feel. Tuesday mornings are for composting. It's smelly but very satisfying work, and you'll learn how we turn kitchen waste into the black gold you can see in those wooden bins over there.

On Wednesday afternoons, school groups visit. We need volunteers to help the children plant and pick, and you certainly don't need to be a teacher. You just need to be patient, and to have a sense of humour.
Thursday evenings are the tool sessions. Some of our spades are older than I am, and a retired carpenter, Mr Abbott, shows people how to mend handles and sharpen blades.

On Friday mornings, we look after the greenhouse. The plants there need watering and checking every few days. You may hear people talk about planting seedlings. That happens on Monday mornings, but it's done by our regular members and a specialist group, so you won't be asked to do it in your first few months.
And finally, Saturday mornings. That's the stall. You'll be serving customers, weighing vegetables and giving advice about what to grow, which is a lot more fun than it sounds.
Well, that's quite enough from me. If you'd like to put on a pair of gloves and follow me round the garden, I'll show you where everything is, and then we'll have another cup of tea.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two apprentices and their trainer review a customer-service training project.
script: Come in, both of you, and sit down. Right, the customer service project. Before we look at your draft, remind me why you ended up choosing complaints handling. I thought you'd both wanted to do something about the online ordering system.
We did at first. Chloe had the idea of looking at the website.

Yes, but then Mr Ferris, our store manager, mentioned at a team meeting that complaints had gone up by nearly a third over the past year, and he asked if anyone could look into it. It seemed better to do something that somebody actually wanted.
And it counted as a real work task, so it can go straight into our portfolios.
Sensible. And how did the interviews with customers go?

Honestly, the hardest bit was getting people to agree to talk to us. We stood by the exit with our clipboards and most of them just walked straight past. Writing everything down wasn't a problem, because we'd practised, and once somebody had agreed they were quite happy to chat, so I'd stopped feeling nervous after the first few. In the end we offered a voucher for a free coffee, and that made a big difference.
That's a good number. And what did you find?
Well, I'd assumed most people would want their money back. In fact, when we asked what would have satisfied them, more than half said they just wanted somebody to apologise properly.
That surprised me too. Waiting times came up quite a lot, but they were a long way down the list.
Interesting. So what about the role-plays? You recorded those, didn't you?

Yes. Chloe played the angry customer and I tried to deal with her. I thought I'd stayed really calm, but when I watched the recording I realised I kept cutting in before she'd finished a sentence. I'd been worried that I spoke too quietly, because I usually do, but you could hear me perfectly well.
Good that you spotted it yourself. Now, before we go through the report, let's sort out the presentation to the store staff next week. Who's doing it?
I suppose I could do the whole thing.
No, we did this together. Why don't I do the survey part, and Dylan does the role-play and the recommendations? Then we'd each have half.

Fine. Twenty minutes in total, and you both take questions at the end. Now, the report itself. The introduction first. It runs to nearly two pages, and nobody needs that much background. Cut it down to half a page.
Then the survey results. I've added up the percentages in your second table and they come to 104.
We could put the results in a chart, which would be easier to read anyway.
A chart is a nice idea, but get the figures right first. You can think about a chart afterwards.

The role-play section is a bit dry. Include a few quotations from the recordings, the actual phrases that worked and the ones that didn't. Real words show the difference far better than your descriptions.
Good idea. I wrote down some of the best ones.
For your recommendations, you've got five, and they're sensible, but they sound rather vague. Give an example for each one, a sentence showing what an assistant could actually say to a customer.
Right. And what about the full interview notes? We've got about ten pages of them.
Don't put them in the main text. Move them to the end as an appendix, for anyone who wants to read them.
Okay. I think that's everything, then.
Yes. Send me the revised version by Friday, and I'll give you a mark for it by the following Wednesday.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of the bicycle and its return to cities.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about the bicycle. It looks like a simple machine, but its history is surprisingly dramatic, and it is now making a remarkable comeback in cities around the world.

Let's begin in 1817. In that year a German inventor built what he called a running machine. It had two wheels in line, a seat and a steering bar, and he made it from wood, although people often assume it was metal, because bicycles of later years were made from iron and steel. The important thing about this machine is what it didn't have. There were no pedals at all. The rider sat astride and pushed along the ground with his feet, rather like a child's balance bike today. It was fun, but not much faster than walking, and the craze faded within a few years.

The great step forward came in the 1860s, when French mechanics fitted pedals directly to the front wheel. The result was faster, but also extremely uncomfortable. The wheels had iron rims, the roads were rough, and the machine soon earned the nickname of the boneshaker.

In the 1870s, makers realised that the bigger the front wheel, the further you travelled with each turn of the pedals. So the wheels grew bigger and bigger, until riders were perched more than a metre and a half above the ground. These high-wheelers, which some of you will know as penny-farthings, were thrilling for young men, but if you hit a stone you were thrown forward over the handlebars, and serious injuries were common.

Then, in 1885, came what is still regarded as the most important design of all, the safety bicycle. It had two wheels of roughly equal size and, this is the key point, the pedals drove the back wheel by means of a chain. Riders sat low down and could put a foot on the ground whenever they wanted.

What really made cycling comfortable, though, was a new kind of tyre. Until the late 1880s, tyres were solid rubber or even iron. Then a Scottish veterinary surgeon, tired of seeing his son's tricycle shake him to pieces, developed air-filled tyres, which we call pneumatic tyres. They absorbed the bumps and were quicker, and within a decade almost every bicycle had them.

The 1890s saw a genuine bicycle craze. Prices fell and clubs sprang up in every town. Campaigners for women's rights said that the bicycle had done more for women than any law. It gave them mobility, but also a new kind of independence, because a woman could now go out alone and decide where she wanted to go.

But the story doesn't have a happy ending, at least not straight away. By the 1960s, the car had taken over. Many cities rebuilt their roads for cars, and cycling came to be seen as old-fashioned. In some countries the number of cycling journeys fell by around 80 percent, and cyclists were squeezed onto narrow edges of the road.

The turning point came in the 1970s. When the price of oil rose sharply, governments began to worry about their dependence on fuel from abroad. At the same time, in the Netherlands, parents were angry about the number of children killed by traffic, and there were mass protests. The result was a programme of safe cycle routes, and within a generation cycling had become normal there again.

Since then, many other cities have followed. One northern European city I looked at recently saw the share of its journeys made by bicycle rise from 5 to 15 percent in just ten years, mainly by separating bikes from traffic with protected lanes. The pandemic then gave cycling another boost.

One last development I'd like to mention is the electric bicycle. A small motor assists the rider, which makes hills much less of a problem, and means that people can carry shopping or children without arriving exhausted. Some critics say that e-bikes are not real cycling, but if they get people out of their cars, I'd say they're a good thing.

So, after two centuries, the bicycle has come full circle, from a wooden toy to a serious answer to the problems of the modern city. In next week's lecture, we'll look at the planning decisions that make cycling safe.

passages.title: Eastgate Swimming Pool: new timetable and pool rules
paras: From Monday 2 September, Eastgate Swimming Pool will introduce a new timetable. The changes follow a survey of more than 600 regular users carried out in the spring, and they are designed to give every group of swimmers a time that suits them.

Weekday sessions. The pool now opens at 6.30 am, half an hour earlier than before, and the main pool is reserved for lane swimming until 8.30 am. From 9.30 until 11.30 am the pool is quieter and ideal for gentle exercise. On Tuesdays and Thursdays this session is for swimmers aged 60 and over; on other days it is open to everyone. School lessons take place in the afternoon, and public swimming begins again at 5.00 pm and continues until 8.30 pm.

Weekends. On Saturdays the pool is open from 8.00 am to 6.00 pm, and the popular Family Splash session, with inflatables and floats, runs from 2.00 pm to 4.00 pm. On Sundays the pool closes earlier, at 2.00 pm, so that the cleaning team can complete their weekly deep clean.

Pool rules. For reasons of safety and hygiene, all swimmers must shower before entering the water. Long hair must be tied back or covered with a swimming cap. Children under 8 must be accompanied in the water by someone aged at least 16, and one adult may supervise no more than two children. Running on the poolside is not permitted, and cameras and mobile phones may not be used anywhere on the poolside.

Lockers. Lockers in the changing area are operated by a £1 coin, which is returned to you when you unlock the locker. Please do not leave valuables unattended on the poolside; the pool cannot accept responsibility for items that are lost or stolen. Showers and changing cubicles are cleaned every hour, and a first-aid room is located next to the main office. Bicycle racks are available by the main entrance. For more information, please ask at reception or visit the pool's website.

passages.title: Fairhaven Furniture Project: collection and delivery
paras: The Fairhaven Furniture Project is a local charity that collects unwanted household furniture, repairs it where necessary and sells it at low prices in our shop on Mill Lane. All the money we raise pays for training places for unemployed young people, who learn to restore furniture in our workshop under the guidance of a skilled carpenter. Last year, more than 40 young people completed the programme, and over half of them went on to find paid work.

What we collect. We are happy to take sofas, armchairs, tables, chairs, wardrobes, bed frames and bookcases, provided they are clean and in reasonable condition. Unfortunately, we cannot accept mattresses, or any item that has been damaged by water or smoke. Electrical goods are not collected by this service.

Free collection. If you live within 15 miles of the shop, our two-person team will collect your furniture free of charge on Tuesdays and Thursdays. To book a collection, phone the shop between 10.00 am and 3.00 pm, Tuesday to Saturday. For items larger than a two-seater sofa, we ask you to email a photograph beforehand so that we can be sure of sending the right vehicle.

Delivery. Customers who buy from our shop can have their purchases delivered on Fridays. The charge is £12 within five miles of the shop and £20 beyond that. Delivery is free for customers who can show a letter confirming that they receive council tax support.
Opening hours. The shop is open from Tuesday to Saturday, 9.30 am to 4.30 pm. Small donations can be brought to the shop during opening hours; there is no need to book.

passages.title: Expenses claims: guidance for staff
paras: A  This policy explains how to claim back money that you have spent on company business. It applies to all permanent and temporary employees. Self-employed contractors are not covered by the policy and should follow the terms of their own contracts. The aim is to make sure that nobody is left out of pocket for genuine business costs, while keeping spending reasonable and fair.

B  Travel. Standard-class rail tickets should be booked in advance whenever possible. Flights must be arranged through the company travel office and not booked personally. Taxis may be claimed only for journeys that begin after 9.00 pm, or when you are carrying heavy equipment. At all other times, please use public transport.

C  Meals and accommodation. When you are working away from home overnight, you may claim up to £8 for lunch and £25 for an evening meal. Alcohol cannot be claimed. Hotels should be booked at a rate of no more than £95 per night, or £130 in London. Please keep your hotel receipt, which must show a breakdown of any extras such as parking or breakfast.

D  Using your own car. If you use your own vehicle for business, you can claim 45 pence per mile for the first 10,000 miles in a tax year and 25 pence per mile after that. You must keep a log of each journey showing the date, the start and finish points and the reason for the trip. Travel between your home and your normal place of work is never claimable.

E  Making a claim. All claims must be submitted through the online portal within 30 days of the date on which the money was spent. Upload a photograph of every receipt. Claims without receipts will not be paid, unless the amount is less than £5.

F  Approval and payment. Claims of more than £250 must be approved by your head of department as well as your line manager. Approved claims are paid with your salary at the end of the month. If a claim contains an error, it will be returned to you with a note explaining what needs to change, and you may then submit it again.

passages.title: Reporting accidents at work
paras: Every accident at work, however small, must be reported. Accurate records help us to identify hazards before somebody is seriously hurt, and the law requires us to keep them. This guidance explains what you should do.

If you are involved in an accident, or see one, your first priority is to make the area safe. Switch off any machinery and warn others to keep away. If somebody is injured, call the nearest first aider, whose name and extension number are displayed beside every lift. In a serious emergency, dial 999 and then inform reception, who will direct the ambulance to the right entrance. Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger.

As soon as possible, and always before the end of your shift, tell your line manager what has happened. The accident must then be recorded, either in the accident book kept at reception or on the online form on the staff intranet. Whichever you choose, include the date, time and place, the names of anyone involved or anyone who saw what happened, and a short description of the cause. Be factual, and do not guess who was to blame.

Accidents that keep a worker away from work for more than seven days, or that cause a serious injury such as a broken bone, must also be reported to the national safety authority within 15 days. The company's safety officer, Ms Brennan, takes care of this, so you do not need to contact the authority yourself.

Incidents in which nobody is hurt, but somebody easily could have been, such as a box falling from a high shelf, are known as near misses. These should be reported in exactly the same way. Many serious accidents are preceded by several near misses, and each report gives us a chance to put things right.

After a report has been made, the safety officer will begin an investigation within five working days and will speak to any witnesses. The investigation may lead to changes, such as new equipment or extra training. You will not be disciplined for reporting an accident honestly. If you have not heard anything within two weeks, please contact the safety officer on extension 4417.

passages.title: Bees in the city
paras: A  On the flat roof of an office block in the centre of a busy city, a dozen white hives stand in a neat row. Between spring and autumn, the occupants of each hive, roughly fifty thousand bees at the height of summer, leave in all directions, flying up to three miles in search of flowers. Ten years ago such a sight would have been rare. Today city beekeeping is thriving, and the number of registered hives in some capitals has doubled in less than a decade. Hotels, banks and universities keep hives on their roofs, and thousands of private individuals have taken up the hobby in back gardens and on allotments.

B  It may seem odd that bees should do well among traffic and concrete, but cities have several advantages over the countryside. Gardens, parks, cemeteries and window boxes together provide a long succession of flowers, from the first crocuses in February to the ivy in November, and the mixture of species is far greater than in a field of a single crop. On farmland, by contrast, there may be a glut of blossom for a few weeks, from oilseed rape in spring for example, followed by a long hungry gap. City buildings also hold the heat, so that the air is a degree or two warmer, which lengthens the season in which bees can forage.

C  Honey from urban hives has been a pleasant surprise. Because the bees visit so many kinds of plants, each harvest has its own character. Honey from a hive near an avenue of lime trees tastes quite different from that of a hive beside a railway line planted with buddleia. Many urban beekeepers sell their jars to neighbours and local cafés, and some earn enough to pay for their equipment. Few, however, make a living from it. The typical hobbyist harvests about ten kilograms from each hive in a good year, and most give much of it away as presents. A few have turned the hobby into a small business, selling candles and polish made from the wax, or running courses for beginners.

D  Getting started is more demanding than many newcomers expect. A hive, protective clothing and a colony of bees cost around £500, and the bees need to be inspected every week from April to September. Most beekeeping associations therefore advise beginners to spend a season working alongside an experienced member before they buy anything. 'People imagine that bees look after themselves,' says one instructor, 'but a colony is a living thing. It can fall sick, run short of food or decide to leave.' The last of these is the most dramatic. When a colony outgrows its hive, half the bees may swarm out and form a dense cluster on a lamp-post or in a garden tree while scouts search for a new home. Swarms are usually harmless, but frightened passers-by often call the emergency services, and a good beekeeper will collect them quickly. Neighbours can also be anxious about stings, so careful keepers place their hives behind a high fence or hedge, which forces the bees to fly upwards and out of everyone's way, and many offer a jar of honey to anyone who lives nearby.

E  Not everyone is convinced that the boom is good news. Honeybees are only one of many thousand species of bee, and most of the others, such as bumblebees, mason bees and a great many tiny solitary species, are wild. Some ecologists argue that, as the number of hives rises, honeybees are taking a growing share of the nectar and pollen in city parks and leaving less for their wild cousins. One study of a large city found that in the districts with the most hives, bumblebees were visiting fewer flowers per hour. The researchers were careful to point out that this does not prove that the hives were the cause, but the finding has troubled many conservationists.

F  A few cities have responded by asking beekeepers to register their hives, and one council has suggested that there should be no more than five hives per square kilometre in its parks. Beekeepers' groups reply that the figure has little evidence behind it, and point out that a single hive on a roof may forage over a much wider area than a ground-level colony would. A more constructive response, in the view of many experts, is to increase the food supply rather than reduce the number of hives. That means leaving lawns uncut, planting herbs and wildflowers in beds that were once bare, and replacing the dull evergreen shrubs outside offices with plants that flower. Several companies that keep hives on their roofs have now planted meadows alongside them.

G  The honeybee itself is in no danger, and nobody suggests that it is. The real value of the urban hive may lie elsewhere. Someone who has followed a colony through a year learns to read the weather, to notice which plants are in flower and to understand how much a single insect depends on its surroundings. Schools that have installed a hive report that children who are nervous at first soon become keen to look after it. Such a person is likely to plant flowers, to think twice before using pesticides and to care about insects of all kinds. If that is so, the answer to the question of whether cities now have too many bees is not to ban hives, but to make sure that there is enough for all of them to eat.

groups.instr: The text has seven paragraphs, A-G. Which paragraph contains the following information? Choose the correct letter, A-G. You may use any letter more than once.

items.q: advice that beginners should learn from an experienced person
items.why: Paragraph D: associations advise beginners to work alongside an experienced member for a season.

items.q: a comparison between the food supply for bees in a city and on farmland
items.why: Paragraph B contrasts a long succession of flowers in the city with a glut and then a hungry gap on farmland.

items.q: an example of companies taking action to help wild bees
items.why: Paragraph F: companies with roof hives have planted meadows alongside them.

items.q: how much honey an average hobby beekeeper produces
items.why: Paragraph C: about ten kilograms per hive in a good year.

items.q: the findings of a study of areas with different numbers of hives
items.why: Paragraph E: in districts with the most hives, bumblebees visited fewer flowers per hour.

groups.instr: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer? Choose YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer, NO if it contradicts the views of the writer, or NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

items.q: Cities offer bees a more varied range of food than farmland does.
items.why: Paragraph B states that the mixture of species in cities is far greater than in a field of a single crop.

items.q: Honey from city hives sells for a higher price than honey from the countryside.
items.why: Prices are not compared; the text says only that some beekeepers sell jars to neighbours and cafés.

items.q: Limiting the number of hives is the best way to protect wild bees.
items.why: The writer says many experts see increasing the food supply, rather than reducing the number of hives, as the more constructive response.

items.q: Keeping bees may make people more concerned about other insects.
items.why: Paragraph G: such a person is likely to 'care about insects of all kinds'.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.q: What does the writer say about people who start beekeeping?
options: They usually give up during the first year.
They can buy the necessary equipment very cheaply.
They often underestimate how much work is involved.
They are advised to start with several colonies.
items.why: Paragraph D says it is more demanding than many newcomers expect, with weekly inspections; equipment costs around £500.

items.q: What does the writer say about swarms?
options: They are usually harmless, though they alarm some people.
They are the main reason beekeepers give up.
They should be left alone until they move on.
They only occur in very large cities.
items.why: 'Swarms are usually harmless, but frightened passers-by often call the emergency services.'

items.q: What point do the researchers in paragraph E make about their study?
options: Honeybees find flowers more quickly than bumblebees.
Bumblebees are declining faster than honeybees.
City parks contain too few flowers for all bees.
It does not prove that the hives caused the result.
items.why: They stressed that the finding does not prove that hives were the cause.

items.q: Which best describes the writer's attitude to the growth in urban beekeeping?
options: alarmed by the damage to wild bees
supportive, but concerned about the food available
doubtful that the trend will last
items.why: The writer welcomes the benefits for people but concludes that the solution is to make sure there is enough for all the bees to eat.
